title: Skydance 拥有所需的一切，唯独缺乏专注
content:
Skydance Has Everything It Needs Except Focus
Skip to content
Weekly Digest
Skydance Has Everything It Needs Except Focus
By Miikka Ahonen •   October 25, 2026
Source: Skydance
In February, Warner Bros.’ gaming boss JB Perrette admitted the company had become distracted by
chasing “too many IPs” across too many studios
. After a series of expensive failures, the company went back to basics and focused on a handful of proven franchises.
Seven months later, there is suddenly more IP to choose from.
On October 6, Paramount Skydance
completed its $110B acquisition
of Warner Bros. Discovery in one of the largest media mergers in history. The newly renamed Skydance now brings together two major Hollywood film studios, two streaming services (Paramount+ and HBO Max), and television networks including CBS, CNN, and HBO. Although the broader implications of the merger are beyond the scope of this article, one detail stands out: almost by accident, Skydance has become a major player in video games.
The original merger announcement barely acknowledged games. On closing day, however,
Skydance combined Paramount’s and Warner Bros.’ gaming businesses under Tony Driscoll
, who had been appointed to lead Paramount Games Studio just four months earlier and now becomes president of Games and Experiences. Driscoll is a veteran of Epic Games, Warner Bros., AT&T, and Disney, and as the company’s head of corporate strategy and development, he led integration plans for the Warner deal.
The IP portfolio is almost absurd. Batman, Harry Potter, Mortal Kombat, Game of Thrones, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, Avatar: The Last Airbender, Star Trek, and SpongeBob now sit under the same roof, alongside some of the industry’s most respected game studios.
On paper, the pieces fit. The reality is a bit messier.
A Complicated Starting Point
It’s easy to say Warner brings game studios and publishing, while Paramount Skydance brings IP and reach. The truth is more nuanced.
Historically, Paramount was primarily a licensor, leaving development and publishing to its partners. Scopely’s
Star Trek Fleet Command
is a good example: a successful live-service mobile game built and operated outside Paramount. The company’s biggest contribution is still its IP portfolio, including TMNT, Star Trek, and Avatar: The Last Airbender.
Meanwhile, Skydance — which merged with Paramount in 2025 — has been quietly building its own games arm. Skydance Interactive specializes in VR experiences and has done so since 2016. Another division, Skydance New Media, was founded in 2019 and is working on ambitious AAA projects including
Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra
and an upcoming
Star Wars
game (notably, both use Disney-licensed IP). Paramount
combined the two under Paramount Games Studio in June
.
WB Games, by contrast, has decades of publishing experience. Its studios include Rocksteady (
Batman: Arkham
), Avalanche Software (
Hogwarts Legacy
), NetherRealm (
Mortal Kombat
), and TT Games (
LEGO titles
). It also operates a meaningful mobile free-to-play business, notably the
Game of Thrones
strategy titles
Conquest
and
Dragonfire.
The track record is impressive. But Warner has spent the past few years learning some expensive lessons.
Suicide Squad: Kill the Justice League
and
MultiVersus
were unsuccessful live-service bets. In 2025, WB Games closed three studios, including Monolith Productions, and
canceled its
Wonder Woman
production
. The publisher subsequently
narrowed its priorities to key franchises
:
Harry Potter
,
Game of Thrones
,
Mortal Kombat
, and
DC
. Warner said it expected that reset to
start paying off in 2027–28
, with new releases from some of its biggest franchises, although beyond a
Hogwarts Legacy
sequel it hasn’t said which titles are coming.
Despite the struggles,
Skydance appears to see games as part of its future
, not just something it got from the merger. That doesn’t mean every studio or project is worth keeping. With roughly
$80B in debt
and a target of “
$6B in annualized run-rate synergies over the next three years
,” Skydance faces some difficult choices. It could invest in its strongest studios, streamline the portfolio, or even sell parts of the business. The risk is cutting valuable development talent instead of weak projects or overlapping functions.
Skydance’s combined games portfolio | Source: Naavik
Where to Bet and Where to Pass
With this much IP under one roof, Skydance has no shortage of opportunities. An open-world
Avatar
RPG, a
Star Trek
grand strategy game, or a premium adventure set in Westeros — almost every franchise could justify an exciting pitch.
The harder part is deciding which ones are worth making, and by whom.
Protect proven teams, not every project.
Hogwarts Legacy
is the prime example. Despite decades of Harry Potter games, nobody had quite delivered the fantasy of actually living in the Wizarding World.
Avalanche finally pulled it off with
Hogwarts Legacy
, selling more than
40M copies
. That kind of expertise is worth protecting.
The same goes for NetherRealm’s
Mortal Kombat
and TT Games’ LEGO specialization. Both have established audiences and know how to serve them.
Rocksteady is a harder call after
Suicide Squad
’s expensive failure. Still, the live-service project doesn’t erase the studio’s
Arkham
pedigree. A return to premium single-player AAA sounds far more promising than another live-service experiment. Arguably,
Suicide Squad
’s biggest problem was the mismatch between the game and the studio’s strengths. Rocksteady wasn’t alone in learning that lesson during the early 2020s live-service craze.
Find the right developer, or don’t make the game.
Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Last Ronin
is a promising example. The game was originally announced in 2023 with Black Forest Games developing and THQ Nordic publishing, but after years of silence, many fans assumed it was dead.
